notes: OWNER CONSTRAINT ON ANY ANSWER, from lamontae at 2026-09-22 15:37:28Z, his words: "people need to decide themselves. and that can change. and their party doesnt solely define their decisions. ust like real life". He said this in answer to this finding. It rules out the obvious answer — that a person's position follows from their party — and it requires that a position be arrived at by the person, that it be able to change afterwards, and that party membership be one input among others rather than the determinant. Added by the research queue lane, which carried his words here verbatim and wrote nothing else into this record; the filing lane owns everything above.

ANSWERED IN PART, 2026-09-22 ~15:43Z, in the director's current reply batch ("TEN-YEAR METRICS CORRECTION"), and it corrects this record's own premise rather than answering the question underneath it. People with no recorded party membership are not thereby politically defective. Six things were counted as one here and must be separated before any number is read again: children; adults not yet eligible; political beliefs held without membership; explicit independence or deliberate nonmembership; actual membership; and uninitialized data. Births and migration must likewise be distinguished from the progressive materialization of people who already existed, which is what this engine actually does. The third party stuck at two members is named as a recruitment and participation chain to inspect, explicitly NOT permission to force an affiliation onto anybody. And a zero count in one sampled run does not prove an event impossible - only a positive-path test and scheduled reachability establish that. The 48% figure in the note above therefore stands as a measurement of what the save records and NOT as evidence that half the world is broken. What remains open is unchanged: what a person draws on to decide a position, and what makes one change.

SETTLED BY THE OWNER, 2026-09-22, and recorded as D-093. His words: "people need to decide themselves. and that can change. and their party doesnt solely define their decisions. just like real life." This is a decision, not one option among several. Three designs are therefore out of scope for any answer: deriving a person's position from their party, because the causation runs the other way or at least not only that way; fixing a position once and never revisiting it, because he has said it can change; and treating party membership as a predictor that decides how somebody votes or acts. What remains open, and is what this request asks, is the mechanism underneath: what a person draws on to decide a position, and what makes one change.

ONE REQUIREMENT, NOT THREE QUESTIONS. This record, what-moves-a-relationship and the blocked conviction work are the same requirement seen from three sides, and answering them separately will produce three unrelated mechanisms. Stated once: a person's own character and history decide their positions; their positions and their conduct decide their relationships; and their party follows from those rather than preceding them. Anything proposed for one side should be checked against the other two.

Measured at de6a71cc, and prompted by a ten-year Kentucky run with nobody doing anything, in which the population nearly doubled from 555 to 1,053 while the share of living people belonging to no party went from 2% to 48%.

WHY THAT HAPPENS, read from source. Party affiliation is written in exactly three places: seated executives at world opening (living-world/opening.ts:390-414), the organizer of a local chapter (party-chapters.ts:195-204), and the consequences of party evolution itself (party-evolution.ts:308, :1056). publicPartyAffiliation otherwise falls back to the party label on a congressional seat roll and returns null when there is none (congress.ts:67-100). So nobody who is not an officeholder or a chapter organizer has ever had a party, and nobody ever acquires one. The 48% is not political drift the simulation modeled; it is the absence of any route.

AND THE SAME GAP ONE LAYER DOWN. Where a person does act politically inside a party, their position is a coin flip. partyActorStance (party-evolution.ts:161-175) forks the world seed on the person id and the question key and picks an option and a strength at random. It reads nothing about the person: no trait, no value, no goal, no life event, no relationship. Stable per person per question across saves, and unconnected to who they are.

THIS IS THE THIRD FACE OF ONE MISSING THING. The conviction layer has three writers whose only caller is the demo, and a belief needs a policy proposition, of which the loaded pack declares none. A person's stance inside a party is a dice roll. A person's party is nothing at all. Each is the same absence: nothing joins a person to a political position.

TWO CONSEQUENCES WORTH NAMING. Party evolution fired once in ten simulated years, and its gate requires both a defining stance and an ally holding the same option who also dissented — three independent coin flips lining up. And a third party founded in year 2 still had two members in year 10, because nothing gives anybody a party, so nothing can give anybody that one.

THE OWNER HAS ALREADY SETTLED THE ADJACENT SHAPE. D-092: being somewhere exposes you to possibly like-minded people, and your actions and personality drive the relationship. An answer here should be consistent with that — a person's politics coming from who they are and what has happened to them, not from a draw.
question: Given that a person decides their own positions, that those can change, and that their party does not decide for them: (1) What should a person draw on to decide where they stand — their temperament, their values, what has happened to them, who is around them, where they live, what their family held? How much should each weigh, and what should it take for two people with similar lives to land in different places? (2) What makes a position change, and at what pace — the same shape as the personality answer he has already settled, where how hard something is to move depends on how strongly it is held? (3) Where should a party then come from: does somebody join the party nearest their positions, or for reasons of their own, and how often should the two disagree? (4) Should most adults have a party at all, and what share should have none — is an unaffiliated 48% wrong, or is the wrong part only that nobody chose it? (5) When is it first decided: at adulthood, on first voting, on being asked, or gradually? (6) How does a new party ever grow past its founders — what makes somebody leave a party they belong to for one that is new?

title: Where an ordinary person's party and political position come from
usableAnswer: A position on each of the six, in plain terms, worked against one example: a thirty-year-old in a mid-sized town with a given temperament and a given upbringing — what party do they hold, why that one, and what would change it. Rough weights rather than exact numbers. Any answer lands on person records, traits and life events that already exist.
whyItMatters: The game is a political simulation in which no ordinary person has any politics. Without an answer here the world becomes less politically readable the longer it runs, a new party can never grow, and the whole conviction layer has nobody to hold a conviction. It is also the owner's stated priority read from the other side: a person's character deciding what happens to them.

answer.summary:
Do not target or repair the reported 48% unaffiliated figure by assigning everyone a party. Separate unknown affiliation, deliberate independence, party sympathy, organizational membership and any jurisdiction-specific registration. Missing producer coverage is a defect; a genuine independent is not.

Actual goals, values, relevant information and lived consequences are primary inputs to a person's issue positions. Family and social history can supply known cues and identification, but not compulsory inherited beliefs. Temperament chiefly influences attention, confidence, openness, approach and expression, not a left/right lookup. Parties offer current platform positions, leadership and activity that people can know and evaluate; party labels must not directly overwrite an individual's views.

For generated adults, produce a coherent prior social/political history where supported rather than wait until their profile is opened. People can remain disengaged; awareness and affiliations can develop at different life stages. For changes, distinguish an issue disagreement, a changed leaning, a formal departure and joining a rival. New parties grow when people actually hear of them, see a reason to engage and choose to join or help; no automatic recruits per elapsed week. Shared workplace or local conditions can create different appraisals, not demographic unanimity.

Example is a test situation, not a fixed character: a thirty-year-old worker hears a colleague's proposal after their schedule changes. Their income needs, existing views, trust in the source and knowledge of the terms are relevant. They might support the proposal while staying with their current party, change their party leaning, or reject the claim. The result must be traceable to those inputs rather than a seeded stance selected solely from their ID.

Acceptance ChatGPT requests (not executed): Hold party fixed and vary meaningful knowledge/goals: an actor can differ on a proposal. Hold actor/state fixed and reopen the screen: no reroll. A known new party can recruit through a real invitation and consent while an unexposed control does not silently join. Independent remains an allowed explicit state.
